631.title: The whirlpool ahead
631.hook: a man swept downstream, warned by someone on the bank
631.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use river and flood images for craving, and some describe the teacher's role, as here, as someone on the bank who can see dangers the practitioner cannot yet see.

segments.voice: Yesterday: conscience and concern. Your line: listen to the small don't. Today, a warning from outside, shouted from a riverbank.

A lazy river on a summer afternoon. Warm water, sun overhead, the current doing all the work. Nobody in the water has to decide anything. That's the picture at the start of a teaching near the end of the Itivuttaka. A man is being carried along by a river that looks lovely and pleasant. He's enjoying it. And then someone standing on the bank, someone who can see further down than he can, starts shouting.
screen: `A LAZY RIVER, A SUMMER AFTERNOON.` → `THE CURRENT DOES THE WORK.` → `SOMEONE ON THE BANK SHOUTS.`

segments.voice: Hey, the man on the bank calls. You're being carried along by a river that looks pleasant. But downstream there's a pool with waves and whirlpools, with dangerous creatures in it. If you reach it, you'll come to grief. And the man in the water, hearing that, struggles against the current with his hands and feet. Then the Buddha explains the picture, piece by piece. The river's current is craving. Its pleasant, alluring look is your own six senses, how good it all seems through them. The pool downstream stands for the five lower fetters, the ties that bind beings to this world. The waves are anger and despair. The whirlpools are the five strands of sense pleasure, the pull of sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches. Turning against the stream is renunciation. Struggling with hands and feet is effort. And the one standing on the bank, who can see what the swimmer can't? That, the Buddha says, is the one who has awakened. You may remember a swimmer from earlier this year, with four dangers in the water: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, sharks. Today the river adds something: the danger doesn't look dangerous. It looks like a nice afternoon. In the picture, the whirlpool can't be seen from the water; it takes someone on the bank. And the swimmer in the story hears, and turns.

segments.voice: Think of a warning someone has given you lately, gently or not, a friend, a doctor, a parent, even your own body, and picture them on the bank, calling. What can they see that you can't from the water? You don't have to swim hard yet; just turn your head toward the bank and listen.

Your line: a stroke toward the bank. The danger in this river looks like a nice afternoon. See you tomorrow.

632.title: First teachers
632.hook: parents are called first teachers, worthy of honor (Itivuttaka 106)
632.howItsDone: In some Buddhist households, especially in Theravada countries, children bow to their parents on special days, and families make offerings or give food to monks in their parents' names as a way of honoring them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a man drifting downstream, a voice from the bank. Your line: a stroke toward the bank. Today the Itivuttaka turns from the river to the family home.

Who taught you to hold a spoon? Nobody remembers the lesson, but somebody gave it, probably more than once, probably with a towel nearby. Before any school, any book, any teacher with a title, there was a pair of hands showing you how the world works: this is hot, this is a cat, this is how you say thank you. One short discourse in the Itivuttaka gives those hands a name. It gives them a teacher's title.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO HOLD A SPOON?` → `BEFORE ANY SCHOOL.` → `A TITLE FOR THOSE HANDS.`

segments.voice: In Itivuttaka 106, the Buddha says that a family where mother and father are honored at home lives with Brahma, the high god of that world. It lives with the first teachers. It lives with those worthy of gifts. These, he says, are terms for mother and father. And he gives the reason in one plain sentence, paraphrased here: parents do much for their children. They bring them up, they feed them, and they show them this world. Show them this world: that's the job description of a first teacher. Not doctrine, not scripture. The world itself: a face, a word, a door, a road. The Pali for first teachers is pubbacariya: pubba, earlier, and acariya, teacher. A teacher's title, and here it goes to the people in the kitchen. The verse at the end gets practical. The wise honor them with food and drink, with clothes and a place to sleep, by bathing them and washing their feet. Care for the body that once cared for yours. Two honest things belong beside this text. First, it speaks of parents as they are meant to be, the ones who raise, feed and show. Not everyone had that, and the text doesn't pretend to describe every home. Some Buddhist teachers widen it to whoever did that work for you: a grandmother, an aunt, a neighbor, a foster parent. Second, the same idea runs through the Buddha's teaching to Sigala, where a grown child supports the parents who once supported them. Honor, here, isn't a feeling first. It's food, clothing, a place to rest.

633.title: In every posture
633.hook: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, keep effort alive (Itivuttaka 110)
633.howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers include walking meditation alongside sitting, and some monastic training asks students to keep mindfulness through all four postures, from walking and standing to sitting and lying down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parents called by a teacher's title. Your line: show them this world. Today the Itivuttaka follows you through the day, from your feet to your pillow.

Walking to the bus, a grudge shows up. Standing in line for coffee, it's still there. Sitting at your desk, you polish it. Lying in bed at night, you rehearse what you should have said. Four positions, one thought, carried all day like a stone in a shoe. The body changes posture a hundred times a day; the mind often doesn't. One discourse near the end of the Itivuttaka walks through exactly those four positions, and asks what you do with a thought like that in each one.
screen: `A GRUDGE AT THE BUS STOP.` → `STILL THERE IN BED.` → `FOUR POSTURES, ONE THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Itivuttaka 110 is built like a walk through the day. If, while a monk is walking, a thought of sensual craving, ill will or harming arises, and he puts up with it, doesn't drop it, doesn't drive it out, then, the Buddha says, he is called lazy, lacking ardor. Then the same sentence for standing, for sitting, for lying down awake. Four times, nearly word for word. Then the other side, four times over: if the thought arises while walking and he doesn't tolerate it, but lets it go, dispels it, ends it, he is called ardent, someone whose effort is alive. The Pali tradition counts these four as the postures, iriyapatha, literally ways of moving; other suttas use them to mean all the time. Notice what the text does not say. It doesn't say the thought shouldn't arise. Thoughts of wanting, of anger, of hurting someone come to everyone, monks included. The line is drawn after: do you let it settle in, or see it and set it down? That's a very different standard from never having the thought at all. And notice why the list repeats. Practice isn't only for the cushion. A sitting meditator who spends the walk home nursing a grudge has done one posture out of four. The closing verse pictures someone who keeps at it, walking or standing, sitting or lying down, and says such a one can reach the highest awakening.
screen: `WALKING, STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN` · `PUTTING UP WITH IT, OR LETTING IT GO` · `THE THOUGHT ISN'T THE PROBLEM` · `NOT ONLY ON THE CUSHION` · then, large: `IN EVERY POSTURE.`

segments.voice: Notice how you're sitting right now: the weight in the seat, the feet on the floor, the hands, and let the spine lift a little, without strain. Then check the mind the same way: is anything being carried, a worry, a grudge, a wanting? If something is there, don't fight it; see it, the way you saw your posture, and loosen your grip on it a little, the way you'd loosen your shoulders.

634.title: As he speaks, he does
634.hook: the Tathagata does as he says and says as he does (Itivuttaka 112)
634.carry: as he speaks, so he does
634.howItsDone: Buddhists in many traditions take the Buddha's consistency of word and deed as a model; monastics in many places recite the rules of training together regularly, partly so that what they say they keep is matched by what they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: walking, standing, sitting, lying down. Your line: effort is alive. Today, the last discourse of the Itivuttaka, and a name explained.

A coach yells at players to stay calm, red in the face. A parent says put the phone away, while scrolling. A friend swears they'll be on time, again. The gap between saying and doing is easy to spot, usually faster in other people than in ourselves. The Itivuttaka's very last discourse names one person in whom, it says, the gap isn't there at all, and it builds one of his titles out of that.
screen: `CALM DOWN, SHOUTED.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN SAYING AND DOING.` → `THE LAST DISCOURSE.`

segments.voice: Itivuttaka 112 lists reasons the Buddha is called Tathagata, a title he uses for himself in the suttas. Tradition reads the word as thus-gone or thus-come, and the discourse plays with it. He has fully understood the world, its arising, its ending, and the way to its ending. From the night of his awakening to the night of his final passing, whatever he says is so and not otherwise. And then the line for today. In Pali it has a lovely rhythm: yathavadi tathakari, yathakari tathavadi. As he says, so he does. As he does, so he says. It runs both directions. Plenty of people do what they say, eventually. Fewer say only what they actually do: no padding, no spin, no talking themselves up. The sutta wants both. That's why, it says, he is called Tathagata, the one who is thus. There's a practical side to this for anyone who isn't a Buddha. Elsewhere the texts tell of the Buddha's teaching to his son Rahula: before you act, while you act, after you act, look at it. Does it match? A life where words and deeds line up has one big advantage: there's nothing to keep track of. No cover stories, no two versions. And it's the end of a collection whose every discourse began, this was said by the Blessed One. It closes with a picture of someone whose saying and doing are the same thing.

635.title: The short books, closed
635.hook: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka
635.howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, such as the discourse on kindness, the jewel discourse and the highest blessings, are among the texts Theravada communities chant regularly, and some Buddhists learn short sayings from these books by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Itivuttaka's last discourse. Your line: as he speaks, so he does. Today the short books close, with a look back.

Some of the best things people say are short. A grandparent's one line at a wedding. A note left on the fridge. A verse someone copied onto a card and kept in a wallet for years. These last weeks lived in books like that: not the long discourses, with their journeys and debates, but three small collections of verses and sayings, some of them only a few lines long. They're shelved together in the Pali canon's Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short texts.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `A VERSE KEPT IN A WALLET.` → `WEEKS OF SHORT BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the Sutta Nipata, which some scholars count among the earliest Buddhist poetry. It opened with a monk shedding the world like a snake sheds its skin. Walking alone like the rhinoceros horn, or with a good friend. The discourse on kindness again, the jewel discourse, and the highest blessings, from caring for parents to a mind unshaken. A boat, the dart of grief, the chapter of eights, and the long road to the far shore. Second, the Udana, inspired sayings, words the Buddha spoke when something moved him. In the seen, only the seen. Boys tormenting fish. The blind men each holding a part of the elephant. And the rare, quiet line: because there is, an escape is known. Third, the Itivuttaka, thus it was said, sayings remembered, the tradition says, by a woman who heard them and repeated them for others. Share even the last bite. Two bright guardians, conscience and concern. The whirlpool ahead. Parents as first teachers. Effort is alive. And word and deed made one. What do the three books share? They're compact; a whole teaching fits in a breath or two. They're made to be memorized and chanted, and some still are. And they're not shallow for being short. A long discourse explains itself. A short verse leaves room, and you have to step into it. Tomorrow a very different kind of book begins, thousands of discourses sorted by subject.

636.title: The Connected Sayings
636.hook: thousands of short discourses gathered by topic
636.howItsDone: Theravada monastics and lay students study the Samyutta Nikaya chapter by chapter, and teachers draw short similes from it for talks, since its discourses are grouped by topic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the short books closed. Your line: short and deep. Today a new block begins, with a very different kind of book.

A hardware store doesn't shelve things by size. Hinges go with hinges, nails with nails, paint with paint, big or small. Walk in needing one little bracket and you know which aisle to try. The early Buddhist community had thousands of short teachings to remember, and at some point someone sorted a great many of them into aisles by topic. That sorted store is the third great collection of the Pali canon: the Samyutta Nikaya.
screen: `A HARDWARE STORE.` → `SORTED BY KIND, NOT SIZE.` → `THOUSANDS OF TEACHINGS, BY TOPIC.`

segments.voice: Samyutta means connected, or yoked together, and nikaya means a collection. So, the Connected Sayings: discourses yoked together by their subject. The Long Discourses were sorted by length. The Middle-Length, more or less by length too. The Samyutta is sorted by kind. All the conversations with devas go in one chapter. All the meetings with Mara in another. The talks with King Pasenadi together; the teachings on feeling, on the five heaps, on the six senses, on the path. There are fifty-six of these chapters, gathered into five books. The first is the book with verses, full of short poems and questions from gods, kings and nuns. The others take on the great themes: how things arise from causes, the heaps, the senses, and finally the path and the four noble truths. Many of the discourses are tiny, a few lines, sometimes just a simile. Here's one, paraphrased, from the chapter on breakthrough. The Buddha picks up a little dust on the tip of his fingernail and asks the monks: which is more, this dust or the great earth? The earth, sir, of course. In the same way, he says, for a disciple who has truly seen the teaching, the suffering already ended is like the earth. What's left is like the dust on a fingernail. That's the whole discourse. Small, sorted, and easy to find again. For the next weeks, one aisle at a time.

segments.voice: Hold up one hand, look at a fingernail, and imagine a few grains of dust on its tip; then let the mind open out to the ground under you, the street, the whole earth, and feel the difference in size. Think of a difficulty you've already come through, something that once felt enormous and is behind you, and let it be the earth. Whatever is still hard today, let it, for now, be the dust.

637.title: Crossing the flood
637.hook: how did you cross? by not halting and not straining (SN 1.1)
637.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe balanced effort as neither too tight nor too loose, and the first discourse of the Samyutta Nikaya is sometimes cited when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Samyutta Nikaya opened. Your line: gathered by kind. Today, its very first discourse, and a week closes.

Late at night, a glow fills the Jeta Grove near Savatthi. A deva, a radiant being from the heavens, has come down to see the Buddha. It bows, stands to one side, and asks the question that opens the whole Connected Sayings. How, dear sir, did you cross the flood? The flood, in these texts, is everything that sweeps a person along: wanting, becoming, views, not knowing. The answer is a handful of words in Pali, and it sounds like a riddle.
screen: `A GLOW IN THE JETA GROVE.` → `HOW DID YOU CROSS THE FLOOD?` → `AN ANSWER LIKE A RIDDLE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers: by not halting, friend, and by not straining, I crossed the flood. The deva asks the obvious thing: how? When I stood still, he says, I sank. When I pushed hard, I was swept away. So, not halting and not straining, I crossed. Take a swimmer in a strong river. Stop moving and you go under. Thrash and fight the current and you wear yourself out and get carried off anyway. What gets you across is steady movement, without either. The Buddhist tradition reads this in many ways. Some commentators say halting means getting stuck in craving and views, and straining means getting carried away by them. Others hear the middle way of the very first sermon, between indulgence and harsh effort. Some meditation teachers just hear practical advice: don't quit, don't force. The deva is delighted. It speaks a verse: after a long time, at last, I see a brahmin, a holy one, fully at peace, who without halting, without straining, has crossed over clinging to the world. Then it bows, circles the Buddha, and vanishes. That's the whole discourse. Look back at this week: a warning shouted from a riverbank, parents named as first teachers, effort kept alive, word and deed matched, the short books closed, the Connected Sayings opened. And now the first of them, back at the water again, with a way across.
screen: `I STOOD STILL AND SANK` · `I PUSHED AND WAS SWEPT AWAY` · `A SWIMMER IN A STRONG RIVER` · `THE DEVA'S VERSE, AND IT VANISHES` · then, large: `NOT HALTING, NOT STRAINING.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be a river: don't stop it, don't push it. When you notice you've drifted off into thoughts, that's halting, so gently start moving again by feeling the next breath; when you notice you're gripping, trying hard to breathe well, that's straining, so soften the shoulders, the jaw, the belly. Not stuck, not forcing: just crossing, one breath at a time.
Ogha, the flood. The first discourse of the Connected Sayings: the Buddha crossed without halting and without straining, because standing still sinks and pushing gets swept away. Today's word.
Your line: not halting, not straining. Steady, the way a swimmer crosses a strong river. That's a week, done.
